**A file carries an error-correcting code so that a flipped bit can be repaired, and a cryptographic
signature so that a changed byte is refused. Both are ordinary. Putting them in the same file forces a
choice that neither feature announces, and one of the two answers is sound only under an assumption that
the error-correcting code exists because it is false.**

The uncomfortable part is that **the two answers are indistinguishable on every input anybody tests**. An
undamaged file behaves identically under both. They diverge only on damaged input, and damaged input is the case the
error-correcting code exists for and the case no test suite exercises, because producing it requires
deliberately corrupting your own artefact.

Enumerating the fault space of a single 64-bit word exhaustively, rather than sampling it, gives four
numbers that decide the design. The space is small enough to enumerate because the number of ways to flip
$w$ bits out of 64 is a binomial coefficient, and for $w \le 4$ it stays under a million.

$$
\binom{64}{1} = 64, \quad \binom{64}{2} = 2{,}016, \quad \binom{64}{3} = 41{,}664, \quad \binom{64}{4} = 635{,}376
\tag{1}
$$

| flipped bits | patterns | repaired exactly | **wrongly "repaired"** | **invisible** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 64 | 64 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 2,016 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 3 | 41,664 | 0 | **23,364 (56.08%)** | 0 |
| 4 | 635,376 | 0 | 0 | **5,133 (0.81%)** |

**Three flipped bits are reported as a successful repair 56.08 percent of the time, and the repair is
wrong every time it happens.** **Four flipped bits are, 5,133 times, completely invisible**, because the
code reports the word as clean when the error pattern is itself a valid codeword.

The consequence is one sentence, and everything else in this article is either its derivation or its
implications.

> **The corrector is not an authority on whether it corrected, and a clean report from it is not evidence
> of integrity.**

### What this is a case study of

The setting is the bytecode format for Keleusma, a language whose value proposition is that a program's
worst-case time and memory can be proven before it runs, and whose compiler backend is described in the
[first][related_post_a369], [second][related_post_a370], [third][related_post_a371] and
[fourth][related_post_a372] articles of this series. **No cryptography background is required, and none of
those articles is a prerequisite.**

The general shape is **composing a repair with a check**, where the check exists to refuse exactly the
class of change the repair performs. That composition has a right order and a wrong one, the wrong one is
what falls out of a natural implementation schedule, and the difference is invisible on the happy path.

The transferable question is **which side of an authentication boundary a transformation sits on**, and
the sharper form this article arrives at is **how long an authentication result stays true**. It is the
same question that separates encrypt-then-authenticate from authenticate-then-encrypt, a question the
cryptographic literature took roughly a decade and several deployed protocol breaks to settle. The answer
here is the same answer, reached from a direction that does not look cryptographic at all.

## What You Need to Know to Read This

**No background is required, and this section is what makes that claim true.** Five ideas carry the whole
article.

**Bits flip.** Storage and memory occasionally return a bit that is not the one written. Radiation,
marginal cells, ageing, electrical noise. This is measured, not hypothetical, and the field studies
are cited later.

**An error-correcting code repairs some of them.** The scheme here is **single-error correction,
double-error detection**, universally abbreviated SECDED. For every 64-bit word of payload it stores 8
extra check bits. Given a word and its check bits it can repair any **one** flipped bit and can notice
that **two** have flipped without saying which. Three or more is outside what it promises, and "outside
what it promises" is not the same as "reported as a failure". That distinction is the whole article.

**A digital signature refuses any change at all.** The publisher signs with a private key and the loader
checks with the public key. Change one bit anywhere the signature covers and verification fails. It does
not repair, it does not localise, it refuses.

**These two mechanisms disagree by construction.** The code exists to accept a damaged file and hand back
a repaired one. The signature exists to reject a damaged file. Put both on one artefact and something must
decide which runs first.

**A scrub is the operation that applies the repair.** Reading the code reports damage, and a scrub walks the
artefact, applies every repair offered, and writes the result back. The name comes from memory
maintenance, where a periodic task rewrites storage so damage does not accumulate until a second fault
lands in a word that already carries one.

## The Setting

The artefact is a compiled module, being one framed buffer holding an instruction stream, an operand pool, and
an auxiliary body with names, constants, type layouts and per-function metadata.

The auxiliary body is a container of **regions**, each a contiguous run of bytes with a kind tag. A parity
plane is itself a region, holding one check byte per 64-bit word of the region it protects, stored
**beside** the data, not interleaved with it. Keeping the payload contiguous is what lets the
reader use a string in place rather than copying it out, and that is load-bearing for a memory bound.

Signing wraps everything, and the implementation says so. The trailer it mentions carries a cyclic
redundancy check, abbreviated CRC, which is a non-cryptographic checksum for accidental damage.

> The signature covers the entire on-disk framed buffer with the signature payload bytes and the CRC
> trailer bytes zeroed.

So the auxiliary body sits **inside** the signed span, and therefore so does every parity plane. That is
the fortunate half of the answer and it was not designed in, since it falls out of signing the whole buffer.

### Notation

**This subsection and the one after it are the algebra, and a reader who wants the argument rather than
the derivation can go straight to The Measurement without losing the thread.** Everything the later
sections rely on is restated there in words and numbers. **The algebra is here because it establishes
that the awkward result is a property of the code itself rather than a defect of this implementation**,
and that is a claim measurement alone cannot make.

Work over the binary field $\mathbb{F}\_2$, where addition is exclusive-or, written $\oplus$.

A codeword is a data word $d \in \mathbb{F}\_2^{64}$ together with $r = 8$ check bits, so the code has
length

$$
n = k + r = 64 + 8 = 72
\tag{2}
$$

and is written $(72, 64)$. The **parity-check matrix** $H \in \mathbb{F}\_2^{8 \times 72}$ has one column
$h_i$ per bit position. The **syndrome** is the short summary the checker computes from a word it has
just read, and **its whole usefulness is that it depends only on what went wrong and not on what the data
was**. For a received word $c$ it is

$$
s(c) = H c^{\top} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{8}
\tag{3}
$$

Write $\mathcal{H} = \{h_0, \dots, h_{71}\}$ for the set of columns, $\mathrm{wt}(x)$ for Hamming weight,
and $d$ for the code's minimum distance.

Let $M$ be the honest artefact as the publisher produced it, $\mathrm{Ver}(X)$ the predicate that the
signature verifies against candidate $X$, and $\mathcal{S}$ the scrub. Let $F_w$ denote a fault of weight
$w$, so $F_w(M) = M \oplus e$ with $\mathrm{wt}(e) = w$.

## The Code, And Why It Behaves As It Does

The construction is not arbitrary and its behaviour on three faults follows from two lines of algebra,
and it is shown because it establishes that the mis-correction result is **structural rather than
a defect of this implementation**.

### Why eight check bits

Every column of $H$ is **distinct** and of **odd weight**. Distinctness is what lets a single fault be
located, because the syndrome equals the column of the flipped bit. Odd weight is what makes the syndrome
self-classifying without a separate overall parity bit.

The number of odd-weight vectors in $\mathbb{F}\_2^{r}$ is exactly half of them,

$$
\bigl|\{x \in \mathbb{F}_2^{r} : \mathrm{wt}(x) \text{ odd}\}\bigr| = 2^{r-1}
\tag{4}
$$

so a code of length $n$ needs

$$
2^{r-1} \ge n = k + r
\tag{5}
$$

With $k = 64$ this gives $2^{r-1} \ge 64 + r$, satisfied first at $r = 8$, where $2^{7} = 128 \ge 72$. At
$r = 7$ it would require $64 \ge 71$, which fails. **Eight is the minimum, not a round number.**

The columns are drawn as the 56 weight-3 vectors and the first 8 weight-5 vectors for the data positions,
and the 8 unit vectors for the check positions.

$$
\binom{8}{3} + 8 = 56 + 8 = 64 \text{ data columns}, \qquad 64 + 8 = 72 = n
\tag{6}
$$

and the supply they are drawn from is

$$
\binom{8}{1} + \binom{8}{3} + \binom{8}{5} + \binom{8}{7} = 8 + 56 + 56 + 8 = 128 = 2^{7}
\tag{7}
$$

so 72 of the 128 available odd-weight vectors are used and 56 are spare. **That ratio is the article's
central number and it reappears below as a prediction.**

### The syndrome is linear, which is what makes an exhaustive sweep cheap

$H$ is a matrix, so $s$ is linear.

$$
s(c \oplus e) = s(c) \oplus s(e)
\tag{8}
$$

For a stored codeword $c$ we have $s(c) = 0$, so the syndrome of a received word depends **only on the
error pattern** and not at all on the data underneath it.

$$
s(c \oplus e) = s(e)
\tag{9}
$$

The instrument checks this instead of assuming it, because everything that follows enumerates error
patterns against a zero data word and would be measuring the wrong space if it failed.

### The decision rule, and the parity argument that decides three faults

The decoder classifies by the syndrome.

$$
\text{classify}(s) =
\begin{cases}
\text{clean} & s = 0\\
\text{correct bit } i & \mathrm{wt}(s) \text{ odd},\; s = h_i \in \mathcal{H}\\
\text{uncorrectable} & \mathrm{wt}(s) \text{ odd},\; s \notin \mathcal{H}\\
\text{uncorrectable} & \mathrm{wt}(s) \text{ even},\; s \neq 0
\end{cases}
\tag{10}
$$

Weight is additive modulo two under exclusive-or,

$$
\mathrm{wt}(a \oplus b) \equiv \mathrm{wt}(a) + \mathrm{wt}(b) \pmod 2
\tag{11}
$$

and every column has odd weight, so for an error of weight $w$,

$$
\mathrm{wt}\bigl(s(e)\bigr) \equiv \sum_{i \in \mathrm{supp}(e)} \mathrm{wt}(h_i) \equiv w \pmod 2
\tag{12}
$$

**The syndrome's parity equals the error's parity.** That single identity explains the entire measured
table.

- $w = 1$ gives an odd syndrome, and it equals $h_i$ exactly. Always corrected, always correctly.
- $w = 2$ gives an even, non-zero syndrome, and always lands in the "uncorrectable" branch. **Never mis-corrected**,
  and that is the guarantee the scheme is named for.
- $w = 3$ gives an **odd** syndrome. It therefore **cannot** be classified as a detected double error. It either
  matches a column and is mis-corrected, or matches nothing and is refused.
- $w = 4$ gives an even syndrome, and it may be **zero**, because the minimum distance is $d = 4$ and weight-4
  codewords exist. A zero syndrome is reported clean.

The simultaneous correction and detection capability of a code of distance $d$ is bounded by

$$
t + s < d, \qquad t = 1,\; s = 2,\; d = 4
\tag{13}
$$

and it is satisfied with no margin. There is nothing left over for a third error, and this is a statement
about distance-four codes in general.

### The prediction, and the measurement that checks it

For a weight-3 error the syndrome is odd, so it falls among the $2^{7} = 128$ odd-weight vectors, of which
$|\mathcal{H}| = 72$ are columns. A crude uniformity assumption predicts a mis-correction fraction of

$$
\Pr[\text{mis-correct} \mid w = 3] \;\approx\; \frac{|\mathcal{H}|}{2^{r-1}} = \frac{72}{128} = 0.5625
\tag{14}
$$

Enumerating all $\binom{64}{3} = 41{,}664$ triple faults exactly gives the following.

$$
\frac{23{,}364}{41{,}664} = 0.5608
\tag{15}
$$

**Nothing in the triple case is unaccounted for**, which is the arithmetic showing the enumeration is
complete rather than merely large.

$$
23{,}364 \ \text{mis-corrected} + 18{,}300 \ \text{refused} = 41{,}664 = \binom{64}{3}
\tag{16}
$$

The heuristic and the measurement differ by less than a fifth of a percentage point.

$$
56.25\% - 56.08\% = 0.17 \ \text{percentage points}
\tag{17}
$$

**The prediction is right to within 0.17 percentage points**, and that matters because it means the
mis-correction rate is a property of the parameters $(n, k, r)$ rather than an accident of which columns
were chosen. A different SECDED code of the same shape would behave the same way.

The weight-4 invisibility count is the number of weight-4 codewords supported entirely on data positions.

$$
\bigl|\{e : \mathrm{wt}(e) = 4,\; s(e) = 0\}\bigr| = 5{,}133 \quad\text{of}\quad \binom{64}{4} = 635{,}376
\tag{18}
$$

a rate of 0.81 percent. **These are corruptions the code declares clean.**

## The Measurement

Two instruments. The first compiles a real module, encodes it with a parity plane per region, injects
faults at chosen positions, scrubs, and compares against the honest artefact byte for byte. The second
enumerates the fault space of one word exhaustively.

**The control comes first, because without it every other line is worthless.** A scrub that does nothing
would report zero corrections on damaged input and look indistinguishable from a scrub that found nothing
wrong. So the clean artefact is scrubbed and required to come back unchanged.

```
artifact 2688 bytes, first protected region at 1872, 32 bytes long

E0 CONTROL clean artifact: corrected=0 uncorrectable=0 identical=true
E1 single fault: 48/48 repaired to a byte-identical artifact
E2 double fault: 4/4 refused; 0 silently mis-repaired
E3 triple fault: 0/6 refused, 6 SILENTLY MIS-REPAIRED, 0 accidentally correct
E4 scrub touches 680 bytes across [1872, 2664) of a 2688 byte artifact; planes are 136 bytes (20.0%)
```

The second instrument checks the linearity identity as its own control, then sweeps.

```
weight  patterns      clean    corrected  uncorrectable   note
     1        64          0           64              0   all repaired exactly
     2      2016          0            0           2016   all detected
     3     41664          0        23364          18300   56.08% MIS-CORRECTED
     4    635376       5133            0         630243   5133 INVISIBLE

triple faults confined to byte 0: 56 of 56 mis-corrected (100.0%)
heuristic prediction 72/128 = 56.25%; measured 56.08%
```

### The exhaustive sweep corrected the sampled one

The six triple faults in E3 all mis-corrected, which reads as a 100 percent rate. **It is not.** The true
rate is 56.08 percent, and the six were all confined to byte 0 of the word, where the rate really is 100
percent, 56 of 56.

That is a **biased sample presented as a measurement**, caught only by enumerating the space. The
qualitative conclusion survives unchanged and the quantitative one was wrong by a factor of nearly two.
The article's threats-to-validity section flagged the sample as hand-chosen before the sweep was run,
and that is the only reason the error was cheap.

### The bias in that sample is the worst case, and the field says it is the likely one

**The 56 patterns confined to one byte are every way of choosing three positions from eight**, so the
conditional sweep is exhaustive over that neighbourhood too.

$$
\binom{8}{3} = 56
\tag{19}
$$

**All 56 mis-correct**, against 56.08 percent unconditionally, so confinement raises the rate by a factor
of nearly two.

$$
\Pr[\text{mis-correct} \mid w = 3, \ \text{one byte}] = 1.0000, \qquad \frac{1.0000}{0.5608} = 1.783
\tag{20}
$$

**This is not a curiosity, because the memory field studies cited later report that faults cluster.** A
fault process that puts three flips in one byte is exactly the process those studies describe, and it is
the process this code handles worst. **The accidental bias in the hand-chosen sample was toward the
physically likely case**, which is the one direction a biased sample is not harmless in.

## Result 1: Repair Is Exact, Which Is What Makes Scrub-Then-Verify Possible

All 64 single-bit error patterns repair to the original word, and 48 of 48 injected into a real artefact
repair it byte for byte.

$$
\mathcal{S}\bigl(M \oplus e\bigr) = M \qquad \text{for all } \mathrm{wt}(e) \le 1
\tag{21}
$$

This is a precondition and it is not automatic. Verifying a signature computed over $M$ against
$\mathcal{S}(X)$ only succeeds if the scrub reproduces $M$ **exactly**, not merely something semantically
equivalent. A scrub that normalised padding, reordered anything, or touched a byte outside the code's
coverage would break verification on honest input and the feature would be unusable.

## Result 2: The Two Orders, And Why The Unsound One Is Subtler Than It Looks

Write $\mathrm{Inst}(X)$ for the bytes the loader ultimately installs and executes. The soundness
condition is that **what runs is what was authenticated**.

$$
\text{accepted}(X) \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathrm{Ver}\bigl(\mathrm{Inst}(X)\bigr)
\tag{22}
$$

The two candidate orders are

$$
\text{verify-then-scrub}\quad \text{accept if } \mathrm{Ver}(X), \;\; \mathrm{Inst}(X) = \mathcal{S}(X)
\tag{23}
$$

$$
\text{scrub-then-verify}\quad \text{accept if } \mathrm{Ver}\bigl(\mathcal{S}(X)\bigr), \;\; \mathrm{Inst}(X) = \mathcal{S}(X)
\tag{24}
$$

**Scrub-then-verify satisfies the condition by construction.** The thing checked and the thing installed are the same
expression.

**Verify-then-scrub is sound if and only if the scrub is the identity on everything that verifies.**

$$
\mathrm{Ver}(X) \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathcal{S}(X) = X
\tag{25}
$$

And here is the part I got wrong in the first draft of this article, and it is shown here rather than
quietly fixed. **That implication holds.** An adversary without the private key cannot produce
$X \neq M$ with $\mathrm{Ver}(X)$, so $\mathrm{Ver}(X)$ forces $X = M$, and the control measurement E0
establishes $\mathcal{S}(M) = M$. **Verify-then-scrub, evaluated at a single instant, is safe.**

The hole is not in the ordering. It is in the word *instant*.

### The real defect is that verification is a statement about a moment

A signature check is not a property the artefact acquires. It is an observation about the bytes as they
were when they were read. Write $X_t$ for the artefact's contents at time $t$. What verify-then-scrub actually
does in a deployed system is

$$
\mathrm{Ver}(X_{t_0}) \quad\text{at load}, \qquad \mathrm{Inst} = \mathcal{S}(X_{t_1}), \quad t_1 > t_0
\tag{26}
$$

and between $t_0$ and $t_1$ the bytes are exposed to exactly the fault process the parity plane was
installed to survive. If $X_{t_1} = X_{t_0} \oplus e$ with $\mathrm{wt}(e) = 3$, then with probability
0.5608 the scrub returns wrong bytes, reports success, and **nothing checks them**, because the only check
ran at $t_0$ against different bytes.

**The probability that this ends in a silently wrong install is a product, and neither factor is zero.**
Writing $\Pr[F_3]$ for the chance that a weight-3 fault lands in the exposed window,

$$
\Pr[\text{wrong bytes installed, reported clean}] = \Pr[F_3] \times 0.5608
\tag{27}
$$

**The article does not estimate the first factor**, because it depends on the storage medium, the
exposure time and the workload, and none of those is measured here. **What it does establish is that the
second factor is not small**, so the product is governed entirely by a quantity the design was built to
assume is non-zero.

**The assumption verify-then-scrub needs is that no fault occurs between the check and the scrub. The parity plane
exists because that assumption is false.** A design cannot rest an argument on the negation of its own
motivation.

This is why verify-then-scrub is the order you build by accident. Three things push toward it and each looks like good
engineering.

**Verification is a load-time concern and scrubbing is a maintenance concern.** They belong to different
phases in every mental model. Load checks the module, and a background task keeps storage healthy. Putting the
scrub after the load is not a decision anyone makes, it is where the code goes.

**Verification is expensive and scrubbing is cheap.** A public-key operation is naturally done once, at
the boundary, with everything after it treated as inside the perimeter.

**The interface makes it the only option.** Reading the load paths of this system shows that the virtual machine is
constructed from an owned module value, the deserialiser takes a shared reference, and the zero-copy path
yields a shared slice. **No load path holds a mutable reference to the artefact bytes.** As the interface
stands, the scrub physically cannot run before verification, because there is nothing for it to write
into. The only place it fits without a new application programming interface is afterwards, and afterwards is
the wrong place.

**The rule that follows is not "scrub first". It is that every scrub must be followed by a fresh
verification**, because a scrub is a modification and the previous verification does not extend over it.

## Result 3: A Clean Error-Correction Report Is Not Evidence Of Integrity

The 5,133 invisible weight-4 patterns make a stronger claim available than the mis-correction result
alone.

$$
\exists\, e,\; \mathrm{wt}(e) = 4,\; s(e) = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{the code reports } M \oplus e \text{ clean}
\tag{28}
$$

**So a clean scrub report does not mean the artefact is undamaged.** It means the damage, if any, was not
of a shape the code notices. For a system that already carries a signature this is a non-issue provided
the signature is the authority. For a system tempted to treat the parity plane as an integrity check in
its own right, and skip the expensive public-key operation when the scrub comes back clean, it is a
complete break.

That temptation is real, because the scrub is cheap and the signature is not. The measurement says the
optimisation is unavailable.

## What A Correct Design Looks Like

The results give five rules. They are stated as rules and not as a design, because the design belongs
to whoever operates the system, and because each rule is traceable to a specific measurement and not to taste.

**One. Every repair is followed by a fresh verification.** Not "scrub first", a phrase that is incomplete,
because that formulation says nothing about a scrub running an hour after load. The invariant is that no
byte is executed which has been modified since the last successful verification. A scrub is a
modification.

**Two. The corrector's report is advisory and the signature is the authority.** A clean scrub must never
be taken as licence to skip verification, however tempting the saving. 5,133 four-bit patterns are
reported clean, and 23,364 three-bit patterns are reported as successful repairs while producing the
wrong word.

**Three. The parity plane is inside the signed span, and that is asserted rather than inherited.** It
holds today because the signature covers the whole framed buffer and the plane lives inside it. Nothing
enforces that relationship, so a future layout change could move the plane out of coverage silently and
turn a denial-of-service vector on with no diagnostic.

**Four. For an encrypted module the scrub operates on ciphertext, before decryption.** Correcting
plaintext modifies data the authenticated-encryption tag has already blessed.

**Five. The interface must offer a path that can repair before it authenticates**, or rule one is
unimplementable and rule two becomes the only defence. This is the concrete change the article asks for
and it is small, being a load path that takes ownership of the artefact bytes or a mutable reference to them.

### What the correct design costs

**One extra signature verification per scrub**, being a public-key operation on a buffer of a few
hundred kilobytes, against a scrub that is a linear pass over the same bytes. If scrubs are periodic and
rare relative to execution, the cost is negligible. If scrubs are frequent, the design has a different
problem, because a system that needs continuous repair is one whose storage is failing rather than ageing.

**Nothing is paid on the honest path.** A module that has not been damaged scrubs to itself and verifies
once, exactly as it does today. The entire cost is incurred in the case that currently either fails to
load or loads something unverified, depending on the order chosen.

## The Plane Must Be Signed, And It Is

There is a second composition question behind the first. The parity plane is data. If it is not covered by
the signature, an adversary supplies a hostile plane and the scrub applies the "corrections" it dictates.

Under scrub-then-verify the signature still catches the result, so integrity holds. It becomes a **denial of
service**, since an attacker who can modify the plane can make a perfectly good module fail to load at will, by
inducing corrections that damage it. An availability attack requiring no key, against a mechanism
installed to improve availability, is worth naming even when integrity is intact.

In this system the plane is inside the signed span, because the signature covers the whole framed buffer
and the plane lives in the auxiliary body. **That is fortunate rather than designed**, and it is the kind
of property that should be pinned by a test rather than inherited from a coincidence of layout.

## The Encrypted Case Has The Same Shape

The system also supports encrypting a module to a recipient, with the signature covering the ciphertext.

> the signature authenticates both the encryption metadata and the ciphertext, so an adversary cannot
> strip the encryption layer and substitute cleartext bytecode while preserving signature validity.

The composition question recurs one level down. Authenticated encryption refuses any modification of the
ciphertext through its own tag, so a scrub must operate on **ciphertext, before decryption**. Correcting
plaintext after decryption modifies data the tag has already blessed, which is verify-then-scrub again in
different clothes.

There is also a mundane and severe practical consequence. **Ciphertext does not tolerate single-bit damage
the way plaintext does.** In counter-mode encryption a single flipped ciphertext bit flips exactly one
plaintext bit, but the authentication tag then fails and the whole module is refused. So for encrypted
modules the parity plane is not an optimisation. It is the only thing between one flipped bit and a module
that cannot be loaded at all.

## The Cost Is Not The Documented Figure

The documented cost is **one check byte per eight payload bytes, so 12.5 percent**. That is the asymptote.
Each plane is a region and each region is padded to a whole word, so for a protected region of $n$ payload
bytes the plane occupies

$$
p(n) = 8 \left\lceil \frac{1}{8}\left\lceil \frac{n}{8} \right\rceil \right\rceil \text{ bytes}
\tag{29}
$$

and the overhead of an artefact with regions $n_1, \dots, n_m$ is

$$
\rho = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{m} p(n_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{m} n_i}, \qquad \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{p(n)}{n} = \frac{1}{8}
\tag{30}
$$

The rounding is per region, so $\rho$ inflates with $m$ and deflates with size. Every artefact here carries
the same $m = 19$ regions regardless of how big it is.

```
E5 plane overhead against the documented 12.5%:
   verify_datalayout    payload      680  planes     136   20.0%   19 regions
   verify_yield         payload    30616  planes    3872   12.6%   19 regions
   codegen              payload   110904  planes   13896   12.5%   19 regions
   parse                payload   303472  planes   37976   12.5%   19 regions
```

$$
\rho = \frac{136}{680} = 0.200, \qquad \frac{0.200}{0.125} = 1.60
\tag{31}
$$

At 680 payload bytes the true cost is **20.0 percent**, sixty percent higher than documented. The figure
is right for the artefacts nobody worries about and wrong for the small ones, and the crossover is quick.

$$
\rho(680) = 20.0\%, \quad \rho(30{,}616) = 12.65\%, \quad \rho(110{,}904) = 12.53\%, \quad \rho(303{,}472) = 12.51\%
\tag{32}
$$

## Threats to Validity

**The sampled measurement was biased and the exhaustive one caught it.** E3's six triple faults reported
100 percent mis-correction against a true rate of 56.08 percent, because all six sat inside byte 0. This
is recorded in the body rather than only here, because it is the most instructive error in the article.

**One code, one implementation.** The exactness result in Result 1 is a property of **this** scrub. The
mis-correction and invisibility results are properties of distance-four codes generally, and the agreement
between the predicted $72/128$ and the measured 0.5608 is the evidence for that generality.

**The exhaustive sweep covers one word, not one artefact.** Faults spanning a word boundary distribute
across two independent syndromes and are not enumerated. Faults landing in the plane rather than the data,
and faults in the region directory, are also outside it. The directory is separately protected by a
triplicated majority vote, a different mechanism with its own composition question this article does not
examine.

**No end-to-end signed artefact was corrupted.** The signature reasoning is derived from reading the
implementation and from the definition of a signature scheme, not from an executed test that signs a
module, damages it and observes the outcome. The signing key material is not reachable from the test
harness as the crate is structured. **This is the weakest link in the article** and the first thing a
reader should be sceptical of.

**The adversary model is not stated formally.** The claims about what an adversary can do assume a
standard existential-unforgeability property and say nothing about an adversary with fault-injection
capability against the loader itself, which the fault-attack literature cited below shows is a real class.

**The vulnerability is prospective.** Nothing in the shipped system calls a scrub at load time today. This
analyses a design decision before it is taken, which is why it is publishable without disclosing anything
exploitable.

## Pattern Extraction

**An authentication result is a statement about a moment, not a property an artefact acquires.** Any
modification after the check invalidates it, including a modification the system performs on itself for
good reasons.

**A mechanism that reports success is not thereby an authority on success.** The scrub returns "corrected"
on 23,364 inputs where it produced the wrong answer, not through a bug but through the definition of the
code it implements. Reading a component's report as a verdict, when its specification covers only part of
its input domain, is the general error.

**A clean report from a partial check is not evidence of the whole property.** 5,133 four-bit patterns are
invisible to a code whose job is noticing damage.

**Two designs that agree on all valid inputs can differ catastrophically on invalid ones**, and the invalid
inputs are the entire reason the feature exists. Every test of an error-correcting code that uses
undamaged data measures nothing about the composition question.

**An interface that makes the unsound order the only convenient one is a design defect**, even before any
code takes the convenient path.

**A hand-chosen sample of a small combinatorial space should be enumerated instead.** $\binom{64}{3}$ is
41,664, a trivial number, and the sample was wrong by nearly a factor of two.

## The Contemporary Literature

**The composition question this article reaches from a storage-reliability direction is a solved problem
in a different field**, and the main value of the survey is that connection. The sections below are
organised by what each body of work contributes to the argument, not by discipline.

**One caveat governs every subsection below and is stated here once rather than repeated in each.** The
harvested works are listed on the strength of their registry metadata and **none of them was read**, so
**no claim in this article rests on any one of them**. The works the argument does rest on are named in
the prose and are a small fraction of what follows. **A hedge repeated on every heading stops being
read**, which is why it appears here instead.

**The sizes are given once, here, rather than restated under each heading**, because thirteen scattered
counts cannot be compared and one table can.

**The shape of that table is itself a finding.** The two literatures this article joins are both large and
both old, while **check-then-use is the smallest cluster by an order of magnitude** and is almost entirely
about file-system races. **The composition question this article asks has been answered in one field and
barely posed in the other.**

### The codes themselves

[Shannon][research_shannon_1948] established that reliable communication over a noisy channel is possible at all, and
[Hamming][research_hamming_1950] gave the first practical construction, a single-error-correcting code built from parity checks
over overlapping subsets of positions. **Golay** gave the perfect codes that bear his name in a famously
short note. The specific construction used here is [Hsiao][research_hsiao_1970]'s, which achieves single-error correction and
double-error detection using minimum-odd-weight columns, improving on the earlier extended-Hamming
approach by removing the need for a separate overall parity bit, and that is why the syndrome is
self-classifying by weight. **MacWilliams and Sloane** is the standard reference for the general theory,
including the distance bounds that make the $t + s < d$ statement above a theorem rather than an
observation. [Bose and Ray-Chaudhuri][research_bose_raychaudhuri_1960] and independently [Hocquenghem][research_hocquenghem_1959] gave the multiple-error-correcting
family, and [Reed and Solomon][research_reed_solomon_1960] the non-binary codes used where burst errors dominate. Both are what one
reaches for when the analysis here shows SECDED is not enough.

[Chen and Hsiao][research_chen_hsiao_1984] surveyed the application of these codes specifically to semiconductor memory, which is
the setting whose vocabulary this article borrows.

### Soft errors are measured, not hypothetical

[May and Woods][research_may_woods_1979] identified alpha particles from packaging materials as a cause of soft errors in dynamic
memory, which is the origin of the field. [Ziegler and Lanford][research_ziegler_lanford_1979] established the cosmic-ray contribution
and its altitude dependence. [Baumann][research_baumann_2005] gives the modern technology-scaling account of why the rate per
bit falls while the rate per device does not.

The large-scale field studies matter more than the physics for a design argument, because they establish
the shape of the fault process, not its cause. [Schroeder, Pinheiro and Weber][research_schroeder_2009] reported error
rates in a large production fleet substantially higher than laboratory predictions, and found errors
strongly correlated with particular modules, not uniformly distributed. [Hwang, Stefanovici and
Schroeder][research_hwang_2012] found repeat errors at the same address to be common, and that is the empirical fact that most
directly threatens the single-fault assumption a SECDED code rests on. [Sridharan and colleagues][research_sridharan_2015]
extended this across several supercomputing installations.

The relevance is direct. **If faults cluster, the multi-bit patterns this article enumerates are not rare
tail events**, and the 56.08 percent mis-correction rate for three faults is reached more often than an
independent-fault model would predict.

### Scrubbing is a known discipline with a known failure mode

[Saleh, Serrano and Patel][research_saleh_1990] analysed memory scrubbing as a reliability technique and established the
basic trade, that periodic rewriting prevents the accumulation of correctable errors into uncorrectable
ones. [Mukherjee and colleagues][research_mukherjee_2003] gave the architectural vulnerability factor methodology for reasoning
about which bits actually matter, which is the counterpart question to this article's, being not whether a bit
flips, but whether anything depends on it.

None of this literature considers a scrub composed with an authentication check, and that is the gap this
article sits in.

### The composition-order problem was settled for encryption, and the answer is the same

[Bellare and Namprempre][research_bellare_namprempre_2000] analysed the three natural compositions of encryption with message
authentication and showed that only encrypt-then-authenticate is generically secure, because the authentication
must cover the **output** of the transformation, not its input. [Krawczyk][research_krawczyk_2001] reached a compatible
conclusion for the transport-layer security record protocol, showing authenticate-then-encrypt secure only
under extra assumptions about the encryption scheme that are not generically available. [Rogaway][research_rogaway_2002]
formalised authenticated encryption with associated data, which is the interface modern constructions
expose.

Substitute "scrub" for "encrypt" and the statement becomes that authentication must cover the output of the
scrub. That is scrub-then-verify.

The reason this took a decade is that the unsound composition **works** until someone attacks it.
[Vaudenay][research_vaudenay_2002] gave the padding-oracle attack, showing that a transformation performed before authentication
leaks through its failure behaviour. [Canvel and colleagues][research_canvel_2003] turned it into a password recovery against
a deployed protocol, [Degabriele and Paterson][research_degabriele_paterson_2007] broke encryption-only configurations of a widely deployed
standard, [Albrecht, Paterson and Watson][research_albrecht_2009] recovered plaintext from a secure-shell implementation, and
[AlFardan and Paterson][research_alfardan_paterson_2013] showed that even a timing side channel in the authenticate-then-encrypt path is
enough. **Marlinspike** compressed the lesson into the practitioner's formulation that performing any
cryptographic operation before verifying authentication reliably ends badly, which generalises past
cryptographic operations to any transformation whose behaviour on adversarial input is unspecified.

### Check-then-use is a named defect in a third field

**[Bishop and Dilger][ref_bishop_dilger]** named the time-of-check-to-time-of-use flaw, in which a program
checks a property of a resource and then acts on the resource, with the property no longer guaranteed to
hold at the moment of action. The classical setting is a race against a concurrent attacker, and the mechanism here is different
in that nothing races, since the artefact is modified by the system itself, deliberately, after the check.

**The structural defect is the same one.** A check establishes a property at $t_0$ and an action assumes it
at $t_1$. That framing is what turned the first draft of this article from a wrong claim into a correct
one.

### Fault injection is the adversarial version of a cosmic ray

[Boneh, DeMillo and Lipton][research_boneh_1997] established that deliberately induced faults break cryptographic
implementations sound under fault-free execution, and [Biham and Shamir][research_biham_shamir_1997] extended the technique to
symmetric ciphers, making fault attacks a general method rather than an arithmetic curiosity.
[Anderson and Kuhn][research_anderson_kuhn_1996] documented the practical attacker capabilities against tamper-resistant hardware,
including low-cost ones, and [Skorobogatov and Anderson][research_skorobogatov_anderson_2002] demonstrated optical fault induction with
inexpensive equipment. **Aumüller and colleagues** gave concrete results and countermeasures for a widely
deployed signature construction, and [Bar-El and colleagues][research_barel_2006] surveyed the area.

The relevance is that **an attacker choosing three bit positions is a far stronger adversary than
radiation placing them at random**, and the 56.08 percent figure is an average over patterns an attacker
does not have to accept. Inside byte 0 the rate is 100 percent.

### Error-correcting memory has already been defeated in exactly this way

[Kim and colleagues][research_kim_2014] showed that software can induce bit flips in memory it does not own, turning bit
flips from a reliability topic into a security topic, and **Seaborn and Dullien** demonstrated privilege
escalation from it. **Razavi and colleagues** showed the flips could be aimed at chosen data, [Gruss and
colleagues][research_gruss_2016] achieved it from a scripting language in a browser, and **van der Veen and colleagues** on
mobile devices. [Frigo and colleagues][research_frigo_2020] later defeated the hardware mitigation deployed in response.

Most directly relevant, [Cojocar and colleagues][research_cojocar_2019] showed that error-correcting memory does not prevent
these attacks, and that **the correction mechanism itself becomes an oracle**, because the timing difference
between a corrected read and a clean read reveals whether a fault was induced, which lets an attacker
search for the multi-bit patterns the code cannot handle. That is the closest published analogue to the
concern raised here, and it establishes the general lesson that **a correction mechanism is part of the
attack surface rather than purely a defence.**

### Authenticating what you execute

[Arbaugh, Farber and Smith][research_arbaugh_1997] gave the chain-of-trust bootstrap architecture in which each stage
authenticates the next before transferring control, which is the discipline scrub-then-verify restates for a
single artefact. **Sailer and colleagues** extended measurement to a running system, and the question of
what happens to a measurement when the measured thing subsequently changes is the same question this
article asks about a scrub. [Necula][research_necula_1997]'s proof-carrying code is the adjacent idea of shipping evidence
with the artefact rather than trusting its origin, and is the tradition this language's verification stance
belongs to.

### Memory integrity verification, where both mechanisms already meet

[Gassend and colleagues][research_gassend_2003] and [Suh and colleagues][research_suh_2003] built architectures that verify the integrity of
memory contents with hash trees while that memory is in active use, which is the setting where an
integrity check and a repair mechanism genuinely have to coexist rather than being composed once at load.
The engineering there assumes the check is re-run on every access, which is the strongest form of the rule
this article derives.

### The standards the signing and encryption rest on

The security notion for signatures is [Goldwasser, Micali and Rivest][research_goldwasser_micali_rivest_1988]'s existential unforgeability under
adaptive chosen-message attack, which is the property the argument in Result 2 uses when it concludes that
$\mathrm{Ver}(X)$ forces $X = M$. The scheme is **Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm**, given by
[Bernstein, Duif, Lange, Schwabe and Yang][research_bernstein_2012] and standardised in **RFC 8032**. The authenticated encryption
is **Galois/Counter Mode**, given by [McGrew and Viega][research_mcgrew_viega_2004] and standardised in **NIST Special Publication
800-38D**, with **Ferguson** and **Joux** documenting the authentication weaknesses that constrain its
parameters.

**None of these specifications addresses composition with an error-correcting layer**, which is
unsurprising and is precisely why the question has to be answered locally.

### The end-to-end argument names this exact placement question

[Saltzer, Reed and Clark][research_saltzer_1984] argued that a function can only be completely and correctly implemented with
the knowledge and help of the application standing at the endpoints, and that placing it in a lower layer
is at best a performance optimisation. That is the general form of this article's conclusion. The parity
plane is a lower-layer integrity mechanism and the signature is the endpoint check. **The plane may make the
endpoint check succeed more often, and it may never substitute for it.**

The argument's authors were explicit that a lower-layer check can still be worth having for performance
reasons, which is exactly the parity plane's real justification, since it converts a load failure into a load
success in the single-fault case, at the cost of 12.5 percent. It buys availability, not integrity.

### Detection codes are weaker than they look, and it has been measured

[Peterson and Brown][research_peterson_brown_1961] introduced cyclic codes for error detection, and [Koopman][research_koopman_2002] established that the
polynomial choice matters enormously and that several widely deployed choices are poor for their intended
message lengths. Most pointedly, [Stone and Partridge][research_stone_partridge_2000] measured real network traffic and found the
checksum and the cyclic redundancy check disagreeing far more often than independence would predict,
concluding that undetected errors reach applications at rates orders of magnitude above the textbook
estimate.

This matters here because the artefact carries a cyclic redundancy check over its prologue and it would
be natural to read that as an integrity mechanism. It covers twelve bytes of header, not the body, and the
literature says that even where such a check does cover data, its detection guarantee is weaker in
practice than its parameters suggest.

### Silent corruption is documented in production storage

[Bairavasundaram and colleagues][research_bairavasundaram_2008] analysed corruption across a very large deployed storage fleet and
found silent data corruption to be real, non-uniform, and correlated with particular devices.
**Schroeder and Gibson** established that observed disk replacement rates substantially exceed vendor
specifications, and [Nightingale and colleagues][research_nightingale_2011] measured hardware failures across a million consumer
machines, finding that a machine that has faulted once is far more likely to fault again.

**Zhang and colleagues** studied a file system that combines checksums with redundancy and repair, which
is the closest deployed analogue to the composition studied here, and found end-to-end integrity holding
only where the check was placed at the boundary that mattered rather than at the convenient one.

The consequence for the fault model is the same one the memory field studies gave. **Faults cluster, so
the multi-bit patterns enumerated above are not tail events**.

### Redundancy and voting, the container's other mechanism

The region directory in this format is protected not by a parity plane but by triplication and a
majority-of-three vote, which is a different mechanism with a different failure profile.
**von Neumann** gave the foundational treatment of building reliable systems from unreliable components
by multiplexing and voting. [Avizienis, Laprie, Randell and Landwehr][research_avizienis_2004] give the taxonomy that separates
fault, error and failure, and is the vocabulary in which "the corrector produced the wrong answer and
reported success" is a fault becoming an error without becoming a detected one. [Siewiorek and Swarz][research_siewiorek_swarz_1998]
is the standard engineering reference for the design space.

A voted directory has the same composition question as a scrubbed region and this article does not
examine it.

### Random bit flips have been harvested in the wild

**Dinaburg** registered domain names one bit away from popular hostnames and measured real traffic
arriving at them, demonstrating that naturally occurring memory errors in end-user machines are frequent
enough to be exploited passively, at scale, with no attacker access to the affected systems.

It is the most concrete available evidence that the fault process this article treats abstractly produces
exploitable events in practice, and it does so without any of the deliberate injection the fault-attack
literature relies on.

### Other transformations composed with cryptography, and how each failed

The pattern of a transformation placed on the wrong side of an authentication boundary recurs, and each
recurrence was discovered by attack rather than by analysis.

[Kelsey][research_kelsey_2002] showed that compressing before encrypting leaks plaintext through ciphertext length, a result
later turned into practical attacks on deployed web protocols under the names CRIME and BREACH.
**Poddebniak and colleagues** showed that email clients which decrypt and then render, without first
verifying integrity, can be made to exfiltrate the plaintext, which is decrypt-then-use in exactly the
shape of verify-then-scrub.

**The recurring lesson is that the unsound composition is discovered by an attacker rather than by a
reviewer**, because it behaves correctly on every honest input.

### Distributing signed artefacts

**Bellissimo, Burgess and Fu** surveyed software update mechanisms and found widespread failures to
authenticate what was installed. [Samuel, Mathewson, Cappos and Dingledine][research_samuel_2010] designed an update framework
around the assumption that individual keys and servers will be compromised, and [Coker and colleagues][research_coker_2011]
set out principles for remote attestation, including that an attestation is a statement about a moment and
that its freshness must be part of what is checked.

**That last principle is this article's conclusion arriving from the attestation literature**, and it is
the strongest external support for the corrected form of the argument in Result 2.

### Bytecode verification, which is this series' own tradition

[Leroy][research_leroy_2003] gave the account of Java bytecode verification and its relationship to type systems, and [Rose][research_rose_2003]
the lightweight variant designed for devices that cannot afford full dataflow analysis, which is the
lineage this language's load-time verifier belongs to. [Haas and colleagues][research_haas_2017] describe a bytecode format
designed from the outset for validation in a single pass. [Leroy][research_leroy_2009]'s verified compiler is the adjacent
result that a transformation can be proven to preserve a property, which is what one would want of a scrub
and is not available for a corrector that mis-corrects by construction.

### Stronger codes, if this one is not enough

The measured multi-bit behaviour makes it reasonable to ask for more. [Gallager][research_gallager_1962]'s low-density
parity-check codes and the **Bose, Ray-Chaudhuri** and **Hocquenghem** family both correct multiple errors,
with [Berlekamp][research_berlekamp_1968] and [Massey][research_massey_1969] supplying the decoding algorithm that made the latter practical. The
trade is decoder complexity and check-bit overhead against the number of errors survived, and it is a
different article.

**None of that changes the composition result.** A stronger code mis-corrects at a higher fault weight
rather than never, so the rule that the corrector must not be the last word is unaffected by the choice.

### What the survey shows

**The survey is 13,796 references and it was assembled by machine**, so the only quantitative use made
of it is the shape of the clusters. Nothing in the argument rests on any single harvested record.

Three things in that shape are worth stating.

**The literature this article needed is not one field, and the two halves barely cite each other.**
Coding theory and soft errors together account for 4,352 records. Cryptographic composition, fault
injection, induced bit flips and attestation together account for 2,890. They are the two halves of the
question, and a reader who knows one of them well is unlikely to know the other. That separation is the
best explanation available for why a composition question with a settled answer in one field arrives
unanswered in the other.

**The smallest cluster is the one the argument turns on.** Check-then-use returns **44 records**, against
2,211 for codes. The time-of-check-to-time-of-use literature is small, old, and almost entirely about
file-system races between concurrent processes. The variant this article describes, where the modifying
party is the system itself and no race is involved, does not appear in it.

**The corpus splits almost evenly across the 2015 boundary**, 7,677 modern against 6,064 earlier. Coding
theory and soft errors are weighted to the earlier period and induced bit flips to the later, which is
the expected shape given Rowhammer dates from 2014.

### The surrounding literature

**A harvested sweep returns a periphery that no single section claims**, and it is reported rather than
discarded. These are works the subject anchors admitted whose subject sits beside one of the twelve
clusters without belonging to it, which for this article means signal integrity, communication coding,
hardware test and the reliability of components other than memory.

## The Source Base

**This is a reading of the primary implementation, a hand-selected primary literature, and a machine
harvest, and the three are not interchangeable.**

**Seventy-four works are hand-selected and cited in the prose**, chosen because a step of the argument
depends on them. **Sixty-five carry identifiers obtained from the registry**, and **nine carry none**
because their venues do not register them. **One of the sixty-six lost its identifier during the
primary-reference review**, when the entry for MacWilliams and Sloane was found to resolve to a different
book and no registered identifier for the work exists, so it is named without a link.

**13,722 further works are harvested and are additional.** They are listed on the strength of their
titles, authors, years and venues as the registry holds them, and **nothing in the argument rests on any
one of them**. A list of thirteen thousand citations otherwise implies a reading it does not represent.

### How the harvested survey was assembled

**120 bibliographic queries across four rounds**, splitting journal articles from proceedings and the
period to 2014 from 2015 onward, because a computing subject that is half coding theory and half security
publishes in both forms and neither round subsumes the other. **39,595 unique identifiers** returned.

The reduction to 13,722 was in two stages and the second is the one that matters.

**A contaminant filter removed 1,799 records**, being 400 by venue, 1,163 by the durable noise patterns in the
repository store, 127 by patterns earned from this sweep, 33 by prior per-record rejections, and 76 whose
verbatim titles fail the corpus prose rules. Deduplication by title and year removed a further **730**
conference-to-journal pairs and repeat registrations, and a junk-title filter removed **237** records of
proceedings furniture, which are front matter and session listings deposited under their own identifiers.

**That left 36,829, and a filter that removes only known contaminants is not a filter.** The first attempt
kept 94 percent, against the 19 percent the previous article in this series kept, and the difference is
that this stage requires a **positive subject anchor** while the first only removed what it recognised.
The anchor gate kept **13,741**, which is 37.3 percent.

**The gate figure and the final figure differ by 19 and the record does not account for the difference.**
The reference list holds 13,722 harvested works against a gate that passed 13,741. **An earlier version of
this section stated 13,788, which is larger than the gate output and therefore impossible**, and the
figure is now taken from a count of the reference list rather than from the pipeline log.

**Every anchor is a compound term or a qualified one, and this subject is unusually badly placed for
bare words.** `code`, `fault`, `signature`, `parity`, `integrity`, `injection`, `trust`, `mask` and
`syndrome` are each shared with a larger literature, four of them enormous, being gene expression signatures in
genomics, medical syndromes, geological faults and medical injections. None appears as a bare anchor.

**Three random samples of the kept and dropped sets were read**, which is where the filters came from.
The samples found contamination in both directions and the corrections went both ways.

- **`Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic`, 73 records.** Philosophy of language, pulled in by
  "verification" and "atomicity". Dropped by venue.
- **Three trade newsletters.** News about security is not security research. Dropped by venue.
- **`Advanced Materials Research` and `Journal of Computer Applications`** look exactly like omnibus
  contamination and are **on subject**, carrying real low-density parity-check and Reed-Solomon work.
  **Not dropped**, which is the reason samples are read before filters are written.
- **`memory error` admitted false-memory psychology.** That anchor was added in an earlier pass to
  recover memory-reliability records the gate was missing, and widening it walked the gate into another
  field. It is now qualified. **A weak anchor is worse than no anchor**, and this is the sweep's own
  instance of a lesson the repository store already recorded.
- **`majority voting` admitted German political science**, and `supply chain` qualified by "software"
  admitted logistics through a paper using "Logware Software". Both are now phrase anchors.

**The residual contamination rate is not zero.** Each sample read during assembly found a family the
previous one had missed, which is the honest expectation for a corpus of this size.

## Epistemic State

**Measured exhaustively, and reproducible from the instrument.** Over one 64-bit word, all 64 single-bit
patterns are repaired exactly, all 2,016 double patterns are detected and none is repaired, and of 41,664
triple patterns, 23,364 are reported as successful corrections and every one produces the wrong word, a
rate of 56.08 percent, with 18,300 refused and none reported clean. Of 635,376 quadruple patterns, 5,133
are reported **clean**, a rate of 0.81 percent. The 56 triple patterns confined to byte 0 mis-correct at
100 percent.

**Measured on a real artefact.** That repairing a single injected fault reproduces the artefact byte for
byte, 48 of 48 across six offsets and eight bit positions. That plane overhead is 20.0 percent at 680
payload bytes and 12.5 percent at 303,472, against a documented 12.5 percent, because each of 19 regions
pads its plane to a whole word.

**Derived, and checkable from the definitions.** That $r = 8$ is the minimum check width, from
$2^{r-1} \ge k + r$. That the syndrome's weight has the same parity as the error's, hence that a
weight-3 error can never be classified as a detected double error. That scrub-then-verify satisfies the soundness
condition by construction. That verify-then-scrub is sound at a single instant, since $\mathrm{Ver}(X)$ forces
$X = M$ and $\mathcal{S}(M) = M$.

**Checked as a control rather than assumed.** That the syndrome map is linear, which is what makes the
exhaustive sweep over error patterns valid independently of the underlying data.

**Read from the implementation, not executed.** That the signature covers the entire framed buffer with
the signature payload and checksum trailer zeroed, hence covers the auxiliary body and every parity plane.
That no load path holds a mutable reference to the artefact bytes, checked across the virtual machine
constructor, the deserialiser and the zero-copy path.

**Imported from the literature rather than established here.** The generic composition result for
authentication. The time-of-check-to-time-of-use framing. The field-study evidence that memory faults
cluster rather than arriving independently.

**Corrected during writing, and left visible.** The first draft claimed verify-then-scrub is a hole outright. That
is wrong, since at a single instant it is safe, because a verifying artefact is the original one and the scrub
is the identity on it. The defect is that verification is a statement about a moment and the scrub acts
later. **Writing the soundness condition as an equation is what exposed the error**, and the corrected
argument is stronger, because it identifies the assumption verify-then-scrub depends on as the negation of the
parity plane's own reason for existing. Separately, the first draft reported a 100 percent triple-fault
mis-correction rate from six hand-chosen patterns, where the true rate is 56.08 percent and the sample was
confined to one byte.

**Verified, and the defect rate is the method's rather than this article's.** All 74 hand-selected
references were resolved against the registry by query, never written from memory. **A bare title query
returned the **wrong work** for eleven of them**, a rate of 14.9 percent, against this series' recorded rates
of 0 of 35, 4 of 27 and 7 of 26. The wrong answers are the instructive part, because each returns a real
registered work with a plausible title, being [`Flip Feng Shui: hammering a needle in the software stack`][ref_flip_feng_shui]
resolved to **`Feng shui research`**, and `The sorcerer's apprentice guide to fault attacks` resolved to a
humanities book chapter called **`5. The Apprentice Sorcerer`**. No reachability check can catch either.

**Adding the authors to the query fixed sixteen and left eight.** Those eight are **not guessed at**, and
the reason is worth recording. **USENIX Security and the File and Storage Technologies conference do not register identifiers for their
proceedings**, so [Efail][ref_efail], [Flip Feng Shui][ref_flip_feng_shui], the
[TCG integrity measurement paper][ref_tcg_ima] and the [ZFS end-to-end integrity study][ref_zfs_e2e]
have no identifier to cite. **A plain bullet is honest where an identifier resolving to
something else is not.**

**Lacking an identifier is not the same as lacking a citation, and the primary-reference pass corrected
that.** Each of those works has a stable publisher page, and four are now cited by it rather than left
unreachable, being **Flip Feng Shui**, the **Trusted Computing Group integrity measurement architecture**, the **ZFS
end-to-end integrity study**, and **Bishop and Dilger**, whose naming of the time-of-check-to-time-of-use
flaw is the closest prior statement of this article's central point and was previously named in bold with
nothing behind it. **Efail was already cited by its project site.**

**A fourth work has no citable identifier of any kind and is now unlinked rather than wrongly linked.**
MacWilliams and Sloane's 1977 book is not registered, and the identifier it carried resolved to a 2004
book chapter called `Group theory and error-correcting codes` in a different book. **It is named in the
prose without a link**, which is the same policy applied above.

**A second self-inflicted error, since it generalises.** The similarity function used to rank those
resolutions folded each title to a single run-on token and therefore scored **zero for identical
strings**, classifying all 74 as doubtful. It failed in the safe direction and was still useless, and it
was caught only because a title that matched the registry verbatim was reported as a mismatch. **A
comparison that cannot return agreement is not a comparison.**

**What this article does not establish.** The behaviour of faults spanning a word boundary, landing in a
plane, or landing in the region directory. Whether a signed artefact, corrupted and scrubbed, actually
verifies, which was reasoned about and not executed. Any rate at which multi-bit faults occur in any real
environment. The correct policy for an uncorrectable region, which is an operational decision rather than
a fact to be measured.

**The strongest claim the evidence supports** is that a scrub must be followed by a fresh verification,
because the corrector returns wrong bytes with a success report on 56.08 percent of three-bit faults and
reports 0.81 percent of four-bit faults as clean, and only the signature distinguishes those from real
repairs.

**The weakest link** is that the signature half of the argument is read rather than run.

## Out of Scope

The choice of policy when a region is uncorrectable, which is operational. The design of a mutable load
path, which this article argues is needed and does not specify. The triplicated majority vote protecting
the region directory, a separate mechanism with its own composition question. Whether a stronger code
should replace SECDED, which the measured multi-bit behaviour makes a reasonable question and which is a
different article. Any claim about fault rates in a particular environment, which is a question about
hardware.

## Conclusion

**A parity plane and a digital signature disagree about what to do with a damaged file, and the
disagreement has a right answer.** Every repair must be followed by a fresh verification, because a
signature check is a statement about the bytes at the moment it ran and a repair changes them afterwards.

The reason this is worth an article rather than a line in a design document is the shape of the trap. **The
wrong arrangement is the one the interface makes convenient**, the two arrangements are indistinguishable
on every undamaged input, and the mechanism that makes the wrong one dangerous is not a bug but the
documented behaviour of the code in use. Nothing about the situation announces itself.

The measurement is what converts this from an argument into a result. **A code that corrects one error and
detects two silently mis-repairs 56.08 percent of three-bit faults and cannot see 0.81 percent of four-bit
ones.** Those numbers are properties of the parameters rather than of this implementation, and they say
that the corrector must never be the last word.

The general form is worth more than the instance. **A component that repairs data is not an authority on
whether it repaired it correctly**, and the check that decides must run afterwards and must cover the
repair. That is the same conclusion the cryptographic literature reached about encryption and
authentication, by a route that had nothing to do with storage reliability.


## Equations

<!-- Equations generated by _lib/equations.py from _sources/equations/. Edit the data file and regenerate. Do not edit this section by hand. -->

This section collects the 32 display equations of the article in the order they appear,
each under its number and reproduced exactly as it stands in the text.
A title in bold names an established result,
and a title in italics beginning with the word Bespoke names a construction made for this analysis.
Of the 32, 15 are established and 17 are bespoke.
Arithmetic on words and syndromes is over the binary field, in which addition is exclusive-or, while counts of patterns and probabilities are ordinary integers and fractions, and the plane overhead is a ratio of bytes that is quoted both as a fraction and as a percentage.

**Equation 1, Number of Fault Patterns of Each Weight.**
The number of ways to flip a given number of bits in a sixty-four-bit word is a binomial coefficient, evaluated here for one to four flipped bits.

$$
\binom{64}{1} = 64, \quad \binom{64}{2} = 2{,}016, \quad \binom{64}{3} = 41{,}664, \quad \binom{64}{4} = 635{,}376
\tag{1}
$$

**Equation 2, Length of the Code.**
A codeword holds sixty-four data bits and eight check bits, so the code has length seventy-two.

$$
n = k + r = 64 + 8 = 72
\tag{2}
$$

**Equation 3, Syndrome of a Received Word.**
The syndrome is the product of the parity-check matrix with the received word, an eight-bit vector that depends only on the error pattern.
[Hamming][research_hamming_1950]

$$
s(c) = H c^{\top} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{8}
\tag{3}
$$

**Equation 4, Number of Odd-Weight Vectors.**
Exactly half of the binary vectors of a given length have odd weight.

$$
\bigl|\{x \in \mathbb{F}_2^{r} : \mathrm{wt}(x) \text{ odd}\}\bigr| = 2^{r-1}
\tag{4}
$$

**Equation 5, Check Bits Needed for Odd-Weight Columns.**
A code whose parity-check columns are distinct and of odd weight needs at least as many odd-weight vectors as it has bit positions, which first holds at eight check bits for sixty-four data bits.
[Hsiao][research_hsiao_1970]

$$
2^{r-1} \ge n = k + r
\tag{5}
$$

**Equation 6, Column Allocation of the Odd-Weight Code.**
The data positions take the fifty-six weight-three columns and eight weight-five columns, and the check positions take the eight unit vectors, which is the minimum-odd-weight construction.
[Hsiao][research_hsiao_1970]

$$
\binom{8}{3} + 8 = 56 + 8 = 64 \text{ data columns}, \qquad 64 + 8 = 72 = n
\tag{6}
$$

**Equation 7, Supply of Odd-Weight Columns.**
Summing the binomial coefficients of the odd weights confirms that one hundred and twenty-eight odd-weight vectors of length eight are available.

$$
\binom{8}{1} + \binom{8}{3} + \binom{8}{5} + \binom{8}{7} = 8 + 56 + 56 + 8 = 128 = 2^{7}
\tag{7}
$$

**Equation 8, Linearity of the Syndrome.**
Because the syndrome is a matrix product over the binary field, the syndrome of a sum is the sum of the syndromes.

$$
s(c \oplus e) = s(c) \oplus s(e)
\tag{8}
$$

**Equation 9, Syndrome Depends Only on the Error.**
A stored codeword has zero syndrome, so the syndrome of a damaged codeword equals the syndrome of the error pattern alone.

$$
s(c \oplus e) = s(e)
\tag{9}
$$

**Equation 10, Syndrome Decoding Rule for Single-Error Correction and Double-Error Detection.**
A zero syndrome is reported clean, an odd syndrome equal to a column is corrected at that position, and every other non-zero syndrome is reported uncorrectable.
[Hsiao][research_hsiao_1970]

$$
\text{classify}(s) =
\begin{cases}
\text{clean} & s = 0\\
\text{correct bit } i & \mathrm{wt}(s) \text{ odd},\; s = h_i \in \mathcal{H}\\
\text{uncorrectable} & \mathrm{wt}(s) \text{ odd},\; s \notin \mathcal{H}\\
\text{uncorrectable} & \mathrm{wt}(s) \text{ even},\; s \neq 0
\end{cases}
\tag{10}
$$

**Equation 11, Parity of Weight Under Exclusive-Or.**
The weight of the exclusive-or of two vectors has the same parity as the sum of their weights.

$$
\mathrm{wt}(a \oplus b) \equiv \mathrm{wt}(a) + \mathrm{wt}(b) \pmod 2
\tag{11}
$$

**Equation 12, Parity of the Syndrome Equals the Parity of the Error.**
Since every column has odd weight, the weight of the syndrome has the same parity as the number of flipped bits.
[Hsiao][research_hsiao_1970]

$$
\mathrm{wt}\bigl(s(e)\bigr) \equiv \sum_{i \in \mathrm{supp}(e)} \mathrm{wt}(h_i) \equiv w \pmod 2
\tag{12}
$$

**Equation 13, Correction and Detection Limit of a Code.**
A code of minimum distance four can correct one error while detecting two only because the sum of the two capabilities is less than the distance, which leaves no margin for a third error.

$$
t + s < d, \qquad t = 1,\; s = 2,\; d = 4
\tag{13}
$$

*Equation 14, Bespoke Uniformity Estimate of the Mis-Correction Rate.*
Assuming that the odd syndrome of a triple fault is uniformly distributed over the odd-weight vectors predicts that the fraction of triple faults mis-corrected is the share of those vectors that are columns.

$$
\Pr[\text{mis-correct} \mid w = 3] \;\approx\; \frac{|\mathcal{H}|}{2^{r-1}} = \frac{72}{128} = 0.5625
\tag{14}
$$

*Equation 15, Bespoke Measured Mis-Correction Rate for Triple Faults.*
Exhaustive enumeration of the triple faults of one word for this implementation gives the fraction that the decoder mis-corrects.

$$
\frac{23{,}364}{41{,}664} = 0.5608
\tag{15}
$$

*Equation 16, Bespoke Accounting of the Triple-Fault Enumeration.*
The mis-corrected and refused triple faults of the enumeration sum to the number of all triple faults, which shows that the enumeration is complete.

$$
23{,}364 \ \text{mis-corrected} + 18{,}300 \ \text{refused} = 41{,}664 = \binom{64}{3}
\tag{16}
$$

*Equation 17, Bespoke Gap Between Prediction and Measurement.*
The uniformity estimate of Equation 14 exceeds the measured rate of Equation 15 by less than a fifth of a percentage point.

$$
56.25\% - 56.08\% = 0.17 \ \text{percentage points}
\tag{17}
$$

*Equation 18, Bespoke Count of Undetectable Weight-Four Errors.*
Enumeration of this code finds the weight-four error patterns on data positions whose syndrome is zero, which the decoder reports as clean.

$$
\bigl|\{e : \mathrm{wt}(e) = 4,\; s(e) = 0\}\bigr| = 5{,}133 \quad\text{of}\quad \binom{64}{4} = 635{,}376
\tag{18}
$$

**Equation 19, Number of Triple Faults Within One Byte.**
Three positions can be chosen from the eight bits of one byte in fifty-six ways.

$$
\binom{8}{3} = 56
\tag{19}
$$

*Equation 20, Bespoke Mis-Correction Rate for Faults Confined to One Byte.*
Enumeration of the triple faults confined to one byte finds that every one is mis-corrected, a rate nearly twice the unconditional rate of Equation 15.

$$
\Pr[\text{mis-correct} \mid w = 3, \ \text{one byte}] = 1.0000, \qquad \frac{1.0000}{0.5608} = 1.783
\tag{20}
$$

*Equation 21, Bespoke Exactness of the Scrub.*
The scrub of this implementation restores the honest artefact byte for byte whenever at most one bit of a word has flipped, a property measured rather than guaranteed by the code.

$$
\mathcal{S}\bigl(M \oplus e\bigr) = M \qquad \text{for all } \mathrm{wt}(e) \le 1
\tag{21}
$$

*Equation 22, Bespoke Soundness Condition for Loading.*
The article requires that any artefact the loader accepts installs bytes on which the signature verifies, so that what runs is what was authenticated.

$$
\text{accepted}(X) \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathrm{Ver}\bigl(\mathrm{Inst}(X)\bigr)
\tag{22}
$$

*Equation 23, Bespoke Verify-Then-Scrub Order.*
In the first order the loader verifies the artefact as read and then installs the scrubbed artefact.

$$
\text{verify-then-scrub}\quad \text{accept if } \mathrm{Ver}(X), \;\; \mathrm{Inst}(X) = \mathcal{S}(X)
\tag{23}
$$

*Equation 24, Bespoke Scrub-Then-Verify Order.*
In the second order the loader scrubs the artefact and verifies the very bytes it installs, which satisfies the soundness condition of Equation 22 by construction.

$$
\text{scrub-then-verify}\quad \text{accept if } \mathrm{Ver}\bigl(\mathcal{S}(X)\bigr), \;\; \mathrm{Inst}(X) = \mathcal{S}(X)
\tag{24}
$$

*Equation 25, Bespoke Condition for Verify-Then-Scrub to Be Sound.*
The first order is sound exactly when the scrub leaves unchanged every artefact on which the signature verifies, which holds at a single instant.

$$
\mathrm{Ver}(X) \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathcal{S}(X) = X
\tag{25}
$$

*Equation 26, Bespoke Verify-Then-Scrub with Separated Times.*
In a deployed system the verification observes the bytes at load and the scrub acts on them later, so a fault in between is installed without any check.

$$
\mathrm{Ver}(X_{t_0}) \quad\text{at load}, \qquad \mathrm{Inst} = \mathcal{S}(X_{t_1}), \quad t_1 > t_0
\tag{26}
$$

*Equation 27, Bespoke Probability of a Silently Wrong Install.*
The probability of installing wrong bytes reported as clean is taken as the product of the unestimated chance of a triple fault in the exposed window and the measured mis-correction rate of Equation 15, which assumes the two are independent.

$$
\Pr[\text{wrong bytes installed, reported clean}] = \Pr[F_3] \times 0.5608
\tag{27}
$$

**Equation 28, Undetectability of an Error Equal to a Codeword.**
An error pattern that is itself a codeword has zero syndrome, so a code of minimum distance four reports some weight-four corruptions as clean.

$$
\exists\, e,\; \mathrm{wt}(e) = 4,\; s(e) = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{the code reports } M \oplus e \text{ clean}
\tag{28}
$$

*Equation 29, Bespoke Size of a Padded Parity Plane.*
Under this format's layout a region of a given number of payload bytes needs one check byte per eight-byte word, and the plane holding those check bytes is padded to a whole word.

$$
p(n) = 8 \left\lceil \frac{1}{8}\left\lceil \frac{n}{8} \right\rceil \right\rceil \text{ bytes}
\tag{29}
$$

*Equation 30, Bespoke Plane Overhead of an Artefact.*
The overhead is the total size of the padded planes divided by the total payload over all protected regions, and it approaches one eighth only as the regions grow large.

$$
\rho = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{m} p(n_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{m} n_i}, \qquad \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{p(n)}{n} = \frac{1}{8}
\tag{30}
$$

*Equation 31, Bespoke Plane Overhead of the Smallest Artefact.*
Equation 30 is evaluated for an artefact of six hundred and eighty payload bytes and compared with the documented overhead of one eighth.

$$
\rho = \frac{136}{680} = 0.200, \qquad \frac{0.200}{0.125} = 1.60
\tag{31}
$$

*Equation 32, Bespoke Plane Overhead Across Artefact Sizes.*
Equation 30 is evaluated for four artefacts of increasing payload, showing the overhead falling toward the documented figure.

$$
\rho(680) = 20.0\%, \quad \rho(30{,}616) = 12.65\%, \quad \rho(110{,}904) = 12.53\%, \quad \rho(303{,}472) = 12.51\%
\tag{32}
$$

### Notation

- $\mathbb{F}_2$, the binary field, in which addition is exclusive-or
- $\oplus$, exclusive-or, bitwise addition over the binary field
- $n$, the code length in bits, except in Equations 29 to 32, where it is the payload of a region in bytes
- $k$, the number of data bits in a codeword
- $r$, the number of check bits in a codeword
- $H$, the parity-check matrix of the code
- $h_i$, the column of the parity-check matrix for bit position $i$
- $\mathcal{H}$, the set of columns of the parity-check matrix
- $s(c)$, the syndrome of a received word $c$, with $s(e)$ the syndrome of an error pattern $e$
- $\mathrm{wt}$, the Hamming weight of a vector, its number of ones
- $\mathrm{supp}(e)$, the set of bit positions at which the error pattern $e$ is one
- $d = 4$, the minimum distance of the code
- $t = 1$, the number of errors the code corrects, with $s = 2$ the number it detects
- $w = 3$, the weight of a fault, the number of bits it flips
- $M$, the honest artefact as the publisher produced it
- $\mathrm{Ver}$, the predicate that the signature verifies against a candidate artefact
- $\mathcal{S}$, the scrub, which applies every repair the code offers
- $\mathrm{Inst}$, the bytes the loader installs and executes
- $X_{t_0}$, the artefact's contents at the time of verification, with $X_{t_1}$ its contents at the later time of the scrub
- $F_3$, a fault of weight three in the window between verification and scrub
- $p(n)$, the size in bytes of the padded parity plane for a region of $n$ payload bytes
- $\rho$, the plane overhead of an artefact, the ratio of plane bytes to payload bytes over its $m$ regions
